On the night of Ramchandra Ray’s escape, Udayaditya makes his way past Sitaram, disarming and binding him so the guard can claim he was overpowered. On the night of Udayaditya’s own escape, Sitaram opens his prison, almost carries him out, and leads him away when Udayaditya is unsure where to go.

Pratapaditya first ordered two Pathans to kill Basanta Ray when he stopped at the Simultali inn on his way to Jessore, but one of them warned him instead. Later, Pratapaditya sent Muktiyar Khan to Raigarh with a written death order, and Muktiyar’s soldier Abdul killed Basanta Ray with a sword.

In the Mahishi’s room in Jessore’s inner quarters, Ramai is disguised as a middle-aged woman when Rammohan seizes and carries him out. Later, in Ramchandra Ray’s room in Chandradwip, he is openly the court jester when Rammohan throws him out.
Rukmini, posing as Mangala, secretly prepares poison disguised as medicine. Surma takes it and dies before she can be exiled.
Her husband takes another wife, leaving Vibha with no place in his palace when she finally arrives.

Rukmini obtains Udayaditya’s signet ring after he offers to give her anything to keep her from sitting on his bed. Sitaram and Bhagavat use its engraved seal to stamp a forged petition that appears to show Udayaditya accusing Pratapaditya of treason to the Emperor to gain the kingdom. Bhagavat presents it to Pratapaditya as a petition intercepted on its way to Delhi, and Pratapaditya orders Udayaditya imprisoned, though he says he does not particularly believe the accusation.

After Udayaditya helped Ramchandra Ray escape, Pratapaditya dismissed two guards involved in the incident, Sitaram and Bhagavat. Udayaditya gave them stipends, but Pratapaditya forbade further help. Surma then secretly sent money to their families. When Pratapaditya learned of it, he ordered her to leave the palace for her paternal home.

The song expresses Basanta Ray’s loneliness and grief for loved ones who are no longer with him. He sings it alone at sunset in Raigarh, remembering the joy of being with them; later, he sings it with Vibha in Jessore, after seeing Surma’s empty room and confronting the family’s loss together.

After failing to stop Udayaditya’s escape, Rukmini tells Pratapaditya that Basanta Ray helped him flee. She then leads Pratapaditya’s men to Raigarh and points out Udayaditya. Pratapaditya has ordered Basanta Ray’s execution, and the soldiers carry it out despite Udayaditya’s pleas.
Pratapaditya receives Ramchandra coolly, with little ceremony or attention. Later, in his own court, Ramchandra allows courtiers to mock Pratapaditya and treat him as far beneath their king.

The widow Rukmini leaves Raigarh, takes the name Mangala, and settles on the outskirts of Jessore. Hoping to reclaim Udayaditya and gain power through him, she cultivates palace servants to learn its affairs. When she learns that Surma may be sent away, she exploits the queen’s request for a remedy to win Udayaditya back: instead, she prepares poison, which kills Surma. After Surma’s death, Rukmini enters Udayaditya’s chamber, appeals to his guilt over their past, and demands his love. He refuses to let her take Surma’s place and gives her his ring to make her leave.

Udayaditya first wishes he had never been crown prince because his father treats him as an heir to be tested rather than a son, and judges him unfit to rule. After later losses leave him grieving and blaming his own weakness, he is brought before Pratapaditya as a prisoner. When his father again says he is unworthy of the kingdom, Udayaditya agrees and asks to be released from the throne. He then swears before Ma-Kali that he will never claim any part of Jessore, sit on its throne, or touch its scepter, leaving Samaraditya as heir while he goes to Kashi.

Ramchandra Ray writes to Pratapaditya saying he has renounced Vibha and she must not be sent to Chandradwip. Rammohan refuses to carry the letter, so Ramchandra gives it to Nayanchand. Afraid to deliver it to Pratapaditya, Nayanchand gives it to the Mahishi instead. She keeps it from Vibha and shows it to Basanta Ray, who advises her to announce that Ramchandra has written asking for Vibha to be sent to Chandradwip. The Mahishi tells Vibha this false version, and Vibha believes her husband has forgiven her and wants her back.

Pratapaditya blocks the canal beside the palace with large sal-wood logs, hoping to trap Ramchandra’s boat. But Rammohan and his men pull the boat up and over the logs. The guards’ stones fall short, they cannot ready a gun, and their pursuit boat arrives too late.

Basanta Ray once turned to his beloved sitar for comfort, but his tears stopped him from playing when he was forced to leave Udayaditya. He left it behind, and later described its strings as broken and impossible to tune. His lost music reflects his loneliness and fading joy; news of Udayaditya’s imprisonment deepens that despair.

Earlier, Udayaditya would confront oppression and protect his subjects without worrying about the consequences. After Surma’s death, fear of Pratapaditya makes him hesitate and withdraw: he abandons plans to prevent an attack, flees when he sees a subject being beaten, and cannot bring himself to help people in need.
Sitaram helps Udayaditya escape the imprisonment caused by the forged petition: while a fire distracts the guards, he opens the prison door and leads him away.

On the first occasion, Rammohan carries Ramchandra Ray on his back down a rope made from knotted sheets, then lowers him into a boat below the palace roof. On the second, after Vibha faints, he lifts her from the palace and places her in a palanquin by the gate.

In Jessore, Vibha is dressed as a richly adorned princess to receive Ramchandra Ray: her mother fills her arms with heavy gold bangles and diamond bracelets, gives her a large nose ring, and styles her hair, despite Vibha’s objections. She is flustered but visibly joyful. In Chandradwip, she refuses a palanquin, dresses as a common woman, and goes to him on foot “like a beggar-woman.” She enters the palace without a welcome and is mistaken for someone seeking alms.

After Surma’s death, the bedchamber window marks her absence: Udayaditya sits beside her empty place and hopes to see her there again. In prison, the small window becomes a source of hope. Through it, he sees the sky and birds and can imagine his own freedom.

Sitaram first seeks loans from Rukmini, flirting with her while promising repayment he never makes. Their relationship turns hostile when Udayaditya is imprisoned: Sitaram blames Rukmini, threatens her, and vows to free him. After arranging Udayaditya’s escape, Sitaram visits Rukmini’s cottage hoping to take her money, believing she is dead. Instead, he finds her alive and furious. She threatens to kill him and goes for a blade; his attempt to revive their affectionate banter only enrages her further. He escapes before she returns with the weapon.

Sitaram and his allies first set the guards’ huts ablaze, drawing the guards away from Udayaditya’s cell. While his men kept the fire going and disrupted efforts to extinguish it, Sitaram led Udayaditya out and helped him reach a boat. He then turned the distraction into a cover-up: his men burned the empty prison cell, and he planted bones, a skull, and Udayaditya’s sword in it. Reports of screams and the cell’s collapse made it appear that Udayaditya had died in the fire, buying Sitaram time before the escape was discovered.

Ramchandra Ray takes Udayaditya’s rescue for granted, believing he acted mainly for his sister Vibha’s sake rather than out of concern for Ramchandra. He feels no gratitude and joins his courtiers in mocking him.

Pratapaditya dismisses his minister’s warnings about the Emperor of Delhi, even when he hears that a complaint against him has been lodged there. Later, Bhagavat and Sitaram forge a petition bearing Prince Udayaditya’s seal, making it appear that the prince has accused his father of treason to the Emperor in hopes of gaining the kingdom. Bhagavat takes it to Pratapaditya instead of Delhi, presenting it as an intercepted petition. The Emperor thus becomes the supposed recipient of Udayaditya’s betrayal, and the forged accusation becomes the means of imprisoning him.

When Surma is present, Vibha turns to her to style her hair as she likes, showing their closeness and Surma’s attentive care. After Surma is gone, Vibha sits waiting for her to braid it, but evening comes and her hair remains unbraided. Later, her unkempt hair becomes a visible sign of the care and comfort missing from the palace.
